<p class="mw-kicker">Marketing in 3 · Issue 43 · Thursday 29 October 2026</p>
<figure class="mw-hero"><picture><source type="image/webp" sizes="(max-width: 900px) 100vw, 900px" srcset="../../images/web/issue-43-brand-followers-960.webp 960w, ../../images/web/issue-43-brand-followers-1600.webp 1600w"><img src="../../images/issue-43-brand-followers.jpg" alt="Three young women at a café table laughing as they look together at a photo on a smartphone, takeaway coffee cups beside them" width="1600" height="900" fetchpriority="high" decoding="async"></picture><figcaption>The feed changes. Why people lean in to look at a brand&#x27;s post together has not. Photo: Vitaly Gariev on Unsplash.</figcaption></figure>
<section class="mw-answer" aria-label="Short answer"><h2>The short answer</h2><div class="mw-ans-grid"><p>The followers who join in are the committed ones. In my survey of 1,356 people who follow brands on social media, a decision tree found that four beliefs about a brand decide how much people read, share and post about it, and commitment to the brand comes first. That produced five kinds of follower, from casual fans who mostly watch to committed fans who create. Feeds are now ranked and partly written by AI, but those four beliefs are still what moves a person to act.</p><div class="mw-ev" role="note" aria-label="Evidence level: 1 of 3 stars, one study"><span class="ev-k">Evidence level</span><ol><li class="on"><span class="ev-s" aria-hidden="true"><b>★</b><i>★</i><i>★</i></span>One study</li><li><span class="ev-s" aria-hidden="true"><b>★</b><b>★</b><i>★</i></span>Several studies</li><li><span class="ev-s" aria-hidden="true"><b>★</b><b>★</b><b>★</b></span>Meta-analysis</li></ol></div></div></section>
<section class="mw-takeaways"><h2>Key takeaways</h2><ul><li>Commitment splits followers first, and every later step depends on which side of that line someone sits.</li><li>Nearly half of followers are brand passionates: they know the brand and think well of it, watch and react, but rarely create.</li><li>The most active creators were committed followers, including a small group who love the brand but do not yet know its full range.</li><li>Followers who know the brand but rate its associations poorly stay quiet, which makes associations the lever to fix first.</li></ul></section>
<section id="what-i-did"><h2>What I did</h2><p>With AI now part of almost every marketing conversation, this felt like the right paper of mine to revisit, so this
time the series looks back as well as forward.</p><p>The question was simple. Brands want followers to read, comment, share and post about them. Most research at the time
looked at people&#x27;s motives. I wanted to know how what people think of a brand turns into what they do with it on social
media, and whether those beliefs sort followers into recognisable types.</p><p>Brand pages in Poland shared my survey with their followers. Each person named a brand they follow and answered questions
about it: how well they know it, what they associate with it, how good they think it is and how loyal they are. They also
said how often they consume, contribute to and create content about it. Instead of averaging effects across everyone, I
used a machine learning method, a conditional inference tree, which keeps splitting people on the belief that best
separates them and ends with rules a manager can read.</p>
<dl class="mw-facts"><div><dt>Sample</dt><dd>1,356 social media users who follow a brand, 56.7% women, average age 29</dd></div><div><dt>Brands</dt><dd>282 brands, from drinks and cars to fashion, beauty, retail and hospitality</dd></div><div><dt>Beliefs measured</dt><dd>12 brand equity items: awareness, associations, perceived quality and loyalty, on 1 to 7 scales</dd></div><div><dt>Behaviour measured</dt><dd>17 items on consuming, contributing to and creating brand content, split into low, medium and high</dd></div><div><dt>Method</dt><dd>Conditional inference tree, controlling for age, gender, social media use and brand</dd></div></dl>
</section>
<section id="commitment-comes-first"><h2>Commitment comes first</h2><p>Out of twelve beliefs, the tree kept four. The first split was commitment, a single statement: &quot;I am committed to this
brand&quot;. People who rated it 5 or above on the 7-point scale went one way, everyone else the other.</p><p>For the committed, the next question was familiarity: do they know the brand well? For the less committed, it was
recognition, then whether the brand&#x27;s associations were favourable. Perceived quality, for all the attention brands give
it, did not make the cut.</p><p>Five end points came out of those splits. Brand passionates (625 people) recognise and like the brand without being
committed. Brand fans (558) are committed and familiar. Low engaged followers (108) recognise the brand but think little
of what it stands for. Brand curious followers (41) have neither commitment nor strong recognition. Prospect brand fans
(24) are committed but only partly familiar with the brand.</p>

<section id="who-creates-and-who-only-watches"><h2>Who creates, and who only watches</h2><p>Brand passionates are the quiet majority. Almost nine in ten consumed brand content at a medium level, and more than half
created little or nothing. They are the audience that watches, likes now and then, and moves on.</p><p>Brand fans did a bit of everything. About one in five contributed at a high level, by commenting and sharing, and almost
as many created content of their own.</p><p>The surprise was the small groups. A third of the brand curious created a lot, in what looked like learning by doing. And
among prospect brand fans, committed but still discovering the range, a third were heavy creators too. Low engaged
followers almost never created anything: two in three stayed at the bottom on creation.</p>

<section id="why-i-think-this-matters-more-in-the-age-of-ai"><h2>Why I think this matters more in the age of AI</h2><p>I collected these data before generative AI was part of every marketing brief. Since then, feeds have been ranked by
recommendation systems, brand posts can be drafted by a model in seconds, and people ask chatbots about brands instead of
searching. It&#x27;s fair to ask whether a survey of brand followers from that era still says anything useful.</p><p>My honest answer is yes, and for a simple reason. The technology decides what lands in front of someone. It does not
decide whether that person feels committed to the brand, recognises it, knows it well or likes what it stands for. Those
are human judgements, built slowly, and they are what turns seeing into joining in. When content becomes cheap and
endless, the scarce thing is not another post. It is a follower who cares enough to answer.</p><p>A second reason makes me fond of this paper now. Much of today&#x27;s AI in marketing is a black box that scores
audiences without saying why. A tree like this one is machine learning you can read: if commitment is high and
familiarity is high, expect a fan. I&#x27;d still choose a model a manager can explain over one they have to trust.</p><p>What I would do differently is test it. The tree describes patterns. It cannot prove that raising commitment causes more
posting, and those people all already followed a brand in one country. If I ran it again, I would add AI-made brand
content to the mix and see whether committed followers respond to it the same way.</p>
</section>
<section id="how-to-apply-it" class="mw-howto"><p class="mw-rsg-kicker">Marketing in 3 steps</p><h2>Ready. Set. Market.</h2><div class="mw-rsg"><div class="mw-phase"><div class="mw-phase-dot" aria-hidden="true">1</div><div class="mw-phase-tag"><span class="mw-phase-name">Ready</span><span class="mw-phase-sub">Decide and prepare</span></div><ul class="mw-rsg-steps"><li><strong>Ask the commitment question first.</strong> Survey a sample of your followers with a single commitment statement, rated from 1 to 7. Treat 5 and above as committed and split everyone else into a second group.</li><li><strong>Add three follow-up questions.</strong> Ask the committed group how well they know your brand. Ask the rest whether they can pick your brand out among others and whether it has favourable associations, each on the same 1 to 7 scale.</li></ul></div><div class="mw-phase"><div class="mw-phase-dot" aria-hidden="true">2</div><div class="mw-phase-tag"><span class="mw-phase-name">Set</span><span class="mw-phase-sub">Build it</span></div><ul class="mw-rsg-steps"><li><strong>Fix associations before asking for posts.</strong> Where people recognise you but score your associations at 3 or below, run content about what the brand stands for, such as values, origin and people, before you ask them to share or create anything.</li><li><strong>Turn passionates into members.</strong> For followers who like you but are not committed, give them a reason to belong: a recurring community format, a members&#x27; perk or a weekly question, run for at least eight weeks.</li></ul></div><div class="mw-phase"><div class="mw-phase-dot" aria-hidden="true">3</div><div class="mw-phase-tag"><span class="mw-phase-name">Market</span><span class="mw-phase-sub">Launch and measure</span></div><ul class="mw-rsg-steps"><li><strong>Widen what committed followers know.</strong> For committed followers who know only part of your brand, show the rest of the range in a short series, one product or service per post, and invite them to post their own use of it.</li><li><strong>Track each group separately.</strong> Every month, count comments, shares and posts from each group. Keep a tactic only if its group&#x27;s activity rises in two months out of three, and re-run the survey every six months.</li></ul></div></div></section>

<section id="what-to-expect"><h2>What to expect</h2><ul class="mw-list"><li><strong>A loud minority.</strong> Most of your creation will come from committed followers, so treat them as partners rather than as an audience.</li><li><strong>A quiet majority that still counts.</strong> Followers who watch and like are the largest group, and they need reasons to belong before they will post.</li><li><strong>Slow movement.</strong> Commitment and associations change over months, not days, so judge the plan by the quarter.</li><li><strong>Less need for volume.</strong> More posts will not move a follower who does not care, so spend effort on the beliefs first.</li></ul></section>
<section id="where-it-does-not-work"><h2>Where it does not work</h2><ul class="mw-list"><li><strong>Patterns, not proof.</strong> The tree finds combinations that go together and cannot show that changing a belief causes more engagement.</li><li><strong>Followers only, one country.</strong> Everyone already followed a brand, and all were recruited through brand pages in Poland.</li><li><strong>Data from before generative AI.</strong> The survey predates AI-made brand content, so how followers respond to it is untested.</li><li><strong>Small groups at the edges.</strong> Two of the five types had fewer than 50 people, so their shares are less certain.</li></ul></section>
<section id="questions"><h2>Questions marketers ask</h2><div class="mw-faq"><h3>What makes people engage with brands on social media?</h3><p>In this study, four beliefs about the brand did: commitment, recognition, familiarity and favourable associations, with commitment the first and strongest split (Schivinski, 2021).</p></div><div class="mw-faq"><h3>What are the five types of brand follower?</h3><p>Brand passionates, brand fans, low engaged followers, brand curious followers and prospect brand fans. Passionates and fans together made up more than eight in ten of the people surveyed.</p></div><div class="mw-faq"><h3>Who posts the most about brands?</h3><p>Committed followers. Fans who know the brand well were consistent contributors, and committed followers who were still learning the range had the highest share of heavy creators.</p></div><div class="mw-faq"><h3>Does this still apply now that AI writes and ranks content?</h3><p>The study predates generative AI, so that part is my view rather than a finding. AI shapes what people see, but whether they act still depends on how they feel about the brand.</p></div><div class="mw-faq"><h3>Can I use the questionnaire?</h3><p>Yes. The brand equity and engagement items are listed on the paper page, together with a free copy of the accepted manuscript.</p></div></section>
<section id="also-new"><h2>Also new this week</h2><div class="mw-also"><article><p class="mw-also-src"><em>Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science</em> · 2026</p><h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s11747-026-01151-7">Free and paid word-of-mouth from physical to digital, AI and beyond</a></h3><p class="mw-also-au">Pauwels &amp; Aksehirli</p><p>A review that updates a well-known study of free word of mouth by setting it beside paid word of mouth, and online talk beside offline talk. It turns fifteen years of research into seven practical questions, from who and why to metrics and methods, and notes where AI and virtual environments change the picture.</p></article><article><p class="mw-also-src"><em>Journal of Research in Interactive Marketing</em> · 2026</p><h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.1108/jrim-04-2026-0303">Can AI outperform humans on Instagram? Evidence from engagement and growth metrics</a></h3><p class="mw-also-au">Freitas</p><p>Comparing 204 matched pairs of AI-run and human-run Instagram accounts, this study finds the same engagement rates and likes, and no gap in comments. AI accounts did gain more followers per post, so synthetic creators help reach, while real conversation stays scarce for both.</p></article></div></section>

Numbers are as reported by the authors; read the article for full methods.</p></section>
